body.p: In response to the Office Action dated April 8, 2024, Claims 1 and 10 have been amended. Claims 12-18 have been added. No new matter is believed to have been added by way of these amendments and new claims.
Accordingly, Claims 1-18 are currently pending for consideration. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration in view of the remarks set forth below.
A. Claim Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 4 103

Claims 1, 3, 9, and 11 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2017/0291602 Al to Newman et al. (hereinafter "Newman") in view of U.S. 9,372,261 to Aoki et al. (hereinafter "Aoki").
Claims 2 and 4 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Newman, Aoki and further in view of U.S. 2010/0033364 Al to Kishida et al. (hereinafter "Kishida").
Claims 5, 7, and 10 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Newman, Aoki and further in view of U.S. 2005/0242985 Al to Ponsford et al. (hereinafter "Ponsford").
Claims 6 and 8 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Newman, Aoki, Kishida and further in view of Ponsford.
1. Rationale of 35 U.S.C. 103

The Patent and Trademark Office has the burden under 35 U.S.C. § 103 to establish aprima facie case of obviousness. The rationale to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious is that all the claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions, and the combination yielded nothing more than predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art. It can be important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine the elements in the way the claimed new subject matter does. If any of these findings cannot be made, then this rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art. MPEP § 2143.

2. Independent Claim 1
Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejection of Claim 1 but has amended the claim to expedite allowance. As amended, Claim 1 recites in part:
a position determiner configured to determine whether the observed points
are in a predetermined proximity extent to each other; and
an eliminator configured to eliminate, in response to determination that the
observed points are in the predetermined proximity extent, all the observed points
from a warning target.
Applicant respectfully asserts that Newman and Aoki, alone or in combination, fail to disclose at least the above feature(s) of amended Claim 1.

For example, Applicant respectfully asserts that the cited references fail to disclose the feature(s) "a position determiner configured to determine whether the observed points are in a predetermined proximity extent to each other". In the rejection of claim 1, the Office alleges that Newman teaches "a position determiner configured to determine whether the observed points are in a predetermined proximity extent" because Newman allegedly discloses "a processor component" which determines if a second vehicle position will "come within a predetermined distance limit".

Without acquiescing to the Office's characterization of Newman in view of the claims, Claim 1 has been amended to recite "a position determiner configured to determine whether the observed points are in a predetermined proximity extent to each other". In contrast, Newman teaches that the predetermined distance limit is a distance of the object relative to the vehicle, which is used to avoid a collision. See Newman, para. [0034] ("thereby detecting that one of the vehicles will contact the subject vehicle, or will come within a predetermined distance limit, if no corrective action is taken."). Applicant respectfully asserts that a predetermined distance limit relative to the vehicle does not teach the observed points being in a predetermined proximity extent to each other, as recited in amended Claim 1. Aoki also fails to remedy the deficiencies of Newman.

Therefore, for at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully asserts that Newman and Aoki, alone or in combination, fail to disclose each and every feature of amended Claim 1. Reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection is respectfully requested.
3. Dependent Claims 2-11

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejections but submits that each of the dependent Claims 2-11 depends directly or indirectly on independent Claim 1. Thus, dependent Claims 2-11 incorporate by reference all the features of independent Claim 1. In view of the features as recited in the independent Claim 1, and in view of the additional features as recited in the dependent claims, Applicant respectfully submits that dependent Claims 2-11 are allowable for at least the reasons discussed above and their respective additional novel features. Although Applicant has not discussed specific features of all of the dependent claims in this response, Applicant does not necessarily agree with the characterizations and assessments made by the Examiner with respect to the dependent claims. Thus, Applicant respectfully submits that dependent Claims 2-11 are allowable.

C. No Disclaimers or Disavowals

Although the present communication may include alterations to the application or claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding in this application that previously pending claims are not patentable. Rather, any alterations or characterizations are being made to facilitate expeditious prosecution of this application. Applicant reserves the right to pursue at a later date any previously pending or other broader or narrower claims that capture

any subject matter supported by the present disclosure, including subject matter found to be specifically disclaimed herein or by any prior prosecution. Accordingly, reviewers of this or any parent, child or related prosecution history shall not reasonably infer that Applicant has made any disclaimers or disavowals of any subject matter supported by the present application.
